title: In praise of end-grain: why we let wood breathe
excerpt: An exploration of moisture equilibrium and how respecting timber movement prevents splitting over decades of seasonal shifts.
content:
Wood never stops breathing. Long after a tree is felled and planed into boards, its cellular structure remains porous, continuously exchanging vapor with the ambient air of the room it occupies.

In our Karen workshop, we treat timber seasoning not as an industrial bottleneck, but as the foundational ceremony of joinery. Every baobab slab, olivewood trunk, and white oak board rests under shade for an average of 18 months before a blade touches its surface.

When furniture fails, it almost never fails from load. It fails from restraint—when rigid glues and steel screws fight against the natural seasonal expansion of the fibers. By employing floating tenons and sliding dovetails, we provide timber the millimeters it demands to expand during Nairobi's wet seasons and settle during the dry heat.

title: Visiting the glass-silvering studio in Industrial Area
excerpt: Behind the curtain of our small silvering laboratory, where molten silver meets hand-blown reed plate for ambient reflections.
content:
Commercial mirrors are made on kilometer-long float glass lines using aluminum sputtering in high-vacuum chambers. The resulting reflection is technically immaculate, razor-sharp, and emotionally cold.

Our mirrors begin with textured architectural reed plate, washed with deionized water and precipitated silver salts applied by hand. The silver adheres unevenly, microscopic molecules bonding with the subtle ripples of the glass.

The reflection produced has depth and warmth. It softens peripheral movement, dampens glare, and mimics the quiet surface of deep forest ponds.

title: The modern home: five rooms designed around quietude
excerpt: Curating architectural calm by pairing warm earth-toned timber anchors with diffuse reflections and tactile organic fibers.
content:
Calm in an interior is not an accident of good fortune; it is an acoustic and optical reality built through materiality.

When hard synthetic surfaces dominate—polished plastics, reflective lacquers, synthetic laminates—sound bounces aggressively and light glares into the eyes. The nervous system remains subtly on alert.

In this photo essay, we document five homes across Nairobi and SoHo where our pieces serve as acoustic diffusers. Hand-scraped timber absorbs reverberation, while fluted glass divides space without severing the path of natural daylight.
